Her tone carries a mix of pride and humor, setting a relaxed vibe at the table.Clavicular responds in a way that keeps the mood steady but adds a different angle.He says, "That is funny because you guys were using a lot of the words in like the South Korean subreddits in like 2014." It’s not confrontational. If anything, it feels like an observation. He points to how certain words and ideas may have traveled across different online spaces over time.Another voice joins in and brings the moment full circle. "Guys, we're like the OGs. I saw a couple of posts about that. We're like copying each other." That line hits in a simple but honest way. It reflects something familiar. Online culture is rarely created in isolation. It grows through sharing, borrowing, and sometimes even unknowingly repeating.That's what makes the clip so powerful. It doesn't want to make a point or win an argument. It only shows a group of people talking, listening, and figuring something out together.This moment feels different in a space where viral content often leads to fights. It reminds people that conversations can be calm, thoughtful, and still important. And sometimes, that honest silence is what makes it work.
Article Summary: A viral clip featuring Clavicular and trans women is gaining attention for its calm and honest tone. The conversation explores how online language and trends move across communities. Viewers are engaging with its thoughtful nature, as it reflects how internet culture evolves through collaboration.

Article Title: Tap and Tapish: A ceramics exhibition celebrate practice and transformation
Article Text:
Aurora Russi, Deputy Head of Mission, Embassy of Italy with Architect Edoardo Fontana at the preview of Tap and Tapish

From Stone to Clay

Artish Vipul Kumar with Reshma Chordia, Founder Art Explore and curator Anita Dube

Artist & Fashion Designer Harpreet Narula

Dilip Cherian with Neelam Pratap Rudy and art collector Lekha Poddar





In a studio in Bhainslana, a village in Rajasthan known for its black marble quarries, artist Vipul Kumar works surrounded by clay, stone, and finished sculptures. Classical music fills the long hours as he returns, day after day, to the same material—shaping, building, and waiting for the kiln to complete what his hands have begun.This is the world behind Tap and Tapish, a new exhibition of ceramic works at Bikaner House, presented by Reshma Chordia's Art Explore and curated by Anita Dube. The title itself speaks to Kumar's artistic philosophy: Tap, sustained practice and discipline; Tapish, the transformative heat of the kiln.Kumar's journey to ceramics was unconventional. He began as a stone carver, learning the language of weight, resistance, and physical labour. That training never left him—it shaped how he approaches clay. What started as an unexpected turn gradually became a lifelong commitment.Tap and Tapish brings together two forces that have shaped Kumar's life: the sustained discipline of practice and the transformative heat that fixes form. The recent works speak to both—sculpture born from repetition, material knowledge, and the permanent mark of fire. Clay offered a different kind of material possibility.It could be built, shaped and changed before entering the kiln, where heat would complete a transformation that the artist had begun by hand: his practice statement reads.Years of working with this material have produced sculpture that moves between abstraction and recognisable form, drawing from mythology, cultural memory, and landscape.Curator Anita Dube describes the works as transforming "the fragility and tenderness of wet clay into a fired strength of bone." It's a phrase that captures the physical heart of the exhibition. Wet clay is vulnerable and responsive. Fire changes its nature permanently. What emerges carries the history of the hand, the material, the time invested, and the heat that finally fixes it.For Kumar, this relationship extends beyond the studio. "The environment is what I am interested in," he has said. His understanding begins with the materials themselves: clay is earth; water makes it workable; air prepares it; fire transforms it. The sculpture becomes part of a much older, elemental process.Reshma Chordia, Director of Art Explore, speaks to the rare quality of Kumar's work: "Vipul builds from where he comes from, and it shows in every surface. The heat of the making is still in it, the weight of hands that know their material. The work carries a rare sensitivity, and it stands with real strength. He works at a scale you seldom see. Expect sculpture that holds its ground and asks you to slow down and stay with it. "This particular rhythm—the distance from metropolitan art centres, the studio at its core—has been essential to his practice. Mentors like Balbir Singh Katt and Himmat Shah shaped his early formation. Encounters with Kabir, Gandhi, and Buddhist thought, alongside experiences in Varanasi and Sarnath, informed his intellectual landscape. Yet Kumar has developed a distinctly individual voice: "I have something to say on my own," he says.The opening saw Delhi's cultural sphere converge—H.E. Mr. Siniša Pavić, Ambassador of the Republic of Serbia; Aurora Russi, Deputy Head of Mission at the Italian Embassy; art collector Lekha Poddar; architect Edoardo Fontana; and notable figures from design and cultural circles.
Article Summary: Tap and Tapish is a new exhibition of ceramic works at Bikaner House, Delhi. It is presented by Reshma Chordia's Art Explore and curated by Anita Dube. The opening saw Delhi's cultural sphere converge. H.E. Siniša Pavić, Ambassador of the Republic of Serbia; Aurora Russi, Deputy Head of Mission at the Italian Embassy.

Article Title: Theatre review: When a doctor ends up needing mercy
Article Text:
A still from the play

Mantra

Want us to review your play? Mail us at tims.delhitimes@timesofindia.com





A poor man named Bhagat, cradling his sick child, walks up to a certain Doctor Chaddha’s house. He beseeches the man to help him and his ailing child. However, Chaddha shoos the man away, asking him to come to his clinic the next day. “I don’t see patients at my residence. And can’t you see, I’m getting ready to play golf? I cannot interrupt my routine.”Bhagat and his friend’s requests fall on deaf ears. In fact, Chaddha doesn’t even listen to his wife, who tries handing him the key to his clinic in an effort to appeal to his good senses.Bhagat’s son dies on the way back home. It was Bhagat and his wife’s seventh and only child. The other six too had passed away, after having fallen prey to various diseases. When the wife hears the news, she goes through the five stages of grief, ably embodied by the actor. The first couple of stages of anger and denial are done in such a raw and realistic manner, that for a moment, one forgets that this in fact, is not a movie, but a live performance.Years later, something tragic happens to Chaddha’s family. His son gets bitten by a snake, and despite being an able doctor himself and unable to help his child in that moment, he calls upon different practitioners of the occult to make his son okay again.Everyone fails.Life had come full circle for Chaddha, who had once shown no mercy to a pleading father. Now Chaddha was on his knees and the news had reached Bhagat, who had a deep knowledge of the occult. This moment, when Bhagat had to decide whether he wanted to show compassion to another helpless father like himself or carry the heavy burden of resentment and anger until he lived, is where director Mannu Singh Rawat’s play becomes most effective in showing that the ties of pain and fury bind us all together. That life has the ability to turn tables at any moment.The stage, though big, relied little on props, lighting and especially music. The drama was driven entirely by Premchand ’s endlessly relevant writing and performances. However, the narration between the scenes felt unnecessary. One of the highlights of the drama was the visually striking chanting sequence.And ultimately,belonged to the actors portraying Bhagat and his wife, who exemplified that a loss this profound is rarely experienced only once.-Anvita Singh
Article Summary: The stage, though big, relied little on props, lighting and especially music. The drama was driven entirely by Premchand ’s endlessly relevant writing and performances. One of the highlights of the drama was the visually striking chanting sequence. The actors portraying Bhagat and his wife exemplified that a loss this profound is rarely experienced only once.

Article Title: Bharat Dabholkar swaps laughs for a chill in Jigsaw, a two-hander thriller that keeps the audience guessing
Article Text:
The ntriguing Hinglish psychological thriller, Jigsaw, captivated audiences during its premiere with a packed house. The play showcases renowned actors Bharat Dabholkar and Damini Chopra, unraveling a gripping narrative set on a stormy night within an isolated dwelling. As the story unfolds, deep-seated secrets and betrayals come to light, challenging perceptions of hero and villain, leaving the audience enthralled by unexpected twists.

A departure for Dabholkar

Two actors, no place to hide

Twists that land





Even on one of the busiest Ganpati visarjan days, the NCPA Experimental Theatre was full on Sunday for the premiere of Jigsaw, Ashvin Gidwani 's new psychological thriller directed by theatre veteran Bharat Dabholkar The Hinglish thriller stars Bharat and Damini Chopra, known for Saaho and Yeh Kaali Kaali Ankhein and runs for roughly 80- 90 minutes. Set over a single rain-soaked evening, Jigsaw brings Ranvijay (Dabholkar) face to face with Ayra (Chopra), the troubled wife of a wealthy businessman, inside an isolated house. What begins as casual conversation turns unsettling as buried truths surface. Secrets, betrayals and unexpected connections emerge, and the balance of power keeps shifting, blurring the line between victim and culprit, justice and revenge. The audience is left asking who is hiding something and who is really in control.Dabholkar has written and directed more than 30 plays across comedy, satire and musicals, including the Bottoms Up series, Oh No! Not Again!! and others. He wrote and directed Jigsaw too, and it is his first thriller. He has said he had never attempted the genre before. While writing the script, he found that almost every page brought another twist, which convinced him the material would work well on stage.The play's most unusual feature is its format. There are no ensemble sequences, dance numbers or frequent set changes. Dabholkar and Chopra are the only two actors and remain on stage almost throughout, so the tension rests on their conversation alone. Dabholkar has described sustaining a play of that length with just two people talking as a major challenge.Chopra, has called the play "one-thrill a minute" and said audiences may think they have worked out what is happening, only to have to rethink their assumptions. Different versions of certain scenes have been rehearsed, so no two performances need feel identical.On opening night, the play held the room from the first scene to the last. Just as the audience settled on a version of events, another revelation undid it, and the two characters kept swapping the upper hand until the final moments. Laughter, gasps and a long silence before the applause suggested the twists landed exactly as intended.
Article Summary: Jigsaw, Ashvin Gidwani's new psychological thriller directed by theatre veteran Bharat Dabholkar. The Hinglish thriller stars Bharat and Damini Chopra, known for Saaho and Yeh Kaali Kaali Ankhein and runs for roughly 80- 90 minutes.

Article Title: Burglars hit Nanded cop’s home, flee with service pistol, 30 bullets, gold & cash
Article Text:
Thieves steal cop’s service pistol, 30 live rounds, cash and gold





Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar: Burglars broke into a police head constable’s home in Nanded ’s Kautha area and escaped with his service pistol, 30 live cartridges, cash and gold worth a total of Rs 16.7 lakh. Police suspect an interstate gang and have deployed six teams to track down three suspects.The burglary took place at Ram Bagh Residency on the intervening night of Friday and Saturday. The house was empty at the time.Nanded SP Neelabh Rohan said, “Preliminary probe has revealed involvement of three suspects. Six teams have been deployed to work on this and nab the suspects.”Head constable Gajanan Baliram Kadam, posted as a crime writer at Nanded city sub-divisional police officer’s office, discovered the burglary when he returned home around 10 am on Saturday.His family had left for their village Gortha on Sept 17 for the Mahalakshmi festival. Kadam returned home on Sept 18 after work and kept his govt-issued pistol and ammunition inside. With his family away, he stepped out for dinner and later returned to his Wazirabad office for work. He worked late and slept at the office, leaving his home vacant.Police suspect the burglars broke open the lock of the second-floor flat during the night.They allegedly ransacked the house and fled with the pistol, ammunition and valuables.When Kadam returned in the morning, he found the front door open and the lock broken. Household articles were strewn around.According to his complaint, the burglars stole Rs 6.5 lakh in cash and a gold necklace, chain and two rings weighing about five tolas and valued at around Rs 5 lakh. The service pistol and 30 cartridges were also missing. The total stolen property has been valued at Rs 16.7 lakh.Senior police officers inspected the spot. An FIR was registered with Nanded Rural police late Saturday after a panchanama.Inspector Omkant Chincholkar, SDPO Prashant Shinde and local crime branch inspector Atul Bhosle visited the scene. Teams from Nanded Rural police and the local crime branch are trying to trace the suspects and recover the stolen weapon and ammunition.Sub-inspector Dnyaneshwar Bhosle is investigating the case.
Article Summary: Head constable Gajanan Baliram Kadam discovered the burglary when he returned home around 10 am on Saturday. The burglars stole Rs 6.5 lakh in cash and a gold necklace, chain and two rings weighing about five tolas and valued at around Rs 5 lakh. The service pistol and 30 cartridges were also missing.

Article Title: Lolge Interschool Cricket Tournament in Sambhajinagar to start from Saturday
Article Text:
A cricket ground

Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar

:





Aspiring cricketers from as many as 20 schools in the district are set for a week-long competition as the Lolge Interschool Cricket Tournament-2026 is scheduled to begin from Saturday.Organised by the Aurangabad District Cricket Association (ADCA) in the memory of the late former president Subhash Lolge, the tournament will see 20 school teams compete across ADCA Ground and Devgiri College Ground till Sept 27.“For students, the biggest attraction this year is guaranteed game time. Every school team will play at least four league matches in the round-robin format, giving young players multiple chances to perform, learn and impress selectors,” Shirish Boralkar, ADCA secretary, said.ADCA president and cabinet minister Atul Save said the aim of the tournament is to provide a quality platform at the school level with proper pitches and competitive exposure.“The cricket-related infrastructure and facilities in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar are set for a major revamp in the near future. It will produce quality players and earn laurels for the city,” he said.The opening ceremony of the tournament will be attended by former Indian cricketer Karsan Ghavri . The semifinals of the tournament will be played on Sept 26 and the final on Sept 27 at ADCA Ground, said organisers.
Article Summary: The Lolge Interschool Cricket Tournament-2026 is scheduled to begin from Saturday. The tournament will see 20 school teams compete across ADCA Ground and Devgiri College Ground. The opening ceremony of the tournament will be attended by former Indian cricketer Karsan Ghavri.

Article Title: 32 years after he walked away, Kolhapur man finally comes home to his 90-year-old mother
Article Text:
Housabai and hos son Khandu who returned after 32 years

Kolhapur:





Thirty-two years ago, Khandu Shripati Sakate walked away from his home in Rukdi village in Kolhapur district. He was 26. His mother did not know if she would ever see him again. This week, at 58, Khandu finally returned home.Waiting for him was his mother Housabai, now 90 and surviving on a pension of just Rs 2,500 a month. She mostly lives alone in a rented room, occasionally staying with relatives. Khandu’s father, who had worked with a farmers’ cooperative, retired and died years ago without seeing his son return.Around 32 years ago, 26-year-old Khandu ran a cycle repair shop in Rukdi. His family was pressuring him to marry, but he did not want to. According to his paternal aunt, he once banged his head against a wall and injured himself, following which he developed mental health issues.Soon afterwards, Khandu left home. The family did not lodge a missing person complaint.For years, there was no word from him.Then, in 2014, Madurai-based Akshaya Trust found Khandu living as a beggar in Chennai. It moved him to a facility for destitute people. There, he was registered as Pandu Sakthi.His path home opened years later through a chance encounter. A team from Shraddha Foundation in Karjat, founded by Ramon Magsaysay Award winner Bharat Vatwani, had travelled to the Madurai facility to drop off another destitute person. Staff there told the volunteers about a man registered as Pandu Sakthi who spoke Marathi.The volunteers took Khandu to Karjat and began his treatment. Within days, he started remembering his past and told the volunteers he desperately wanted to go home.“He told us that he used to live in Rukadi and talked about his parents, especially father. We carried out search and found his mother Housabai living alone in a rented house. We further enquired among relatives and neighbors and matched the claims,” said Ajay Ransure, a social worker with Shraddha Foundation.“We have reunited him with his mother and relatives. We have given him medicines he will need for two months and will continue to monitor health and provide medicines for next two years,” Ransure said.
Article Summary: Khandu Shripati Sakate walked away from his home in Rukdi village in Kolhapur district when he was 26. His mother Housabai, now 90 and surviving on a pension of just Rs 2,500 a month, lives alone in a rented room. Khandu’s father, who had worked with a farmers’ cooperative, retired and died years ago without seeing his son return.

Article Title: Ganpatipule Temple caps knee-length attire rule for devotees from New Year
Article Text:
Under the guidelines, men and women must wear attire extending below the knees to enter the temple

Kolhapur

:





Devotees visiting the Ganpatipule temple in Ratnagiri district will have to follow a mandatory dress code starting Jan 1, 2027, as the temple trust moves to strictly enforce norms aimed at preserving the sanctity of the place of worship.Under the new guidelines, both men and women must wear attire that extends below the knees to enter the temple. Shorts, skirts, and dresses above knee length, along with clothing featuring “vulgar messages” or prints, will be strictly prohibited. Children below the age of 10 have been exempted from this rule.Notices detailing the norms have already been displayed outside the temple premises. Temple authorities stated that the decision was prompted by an increasing number of devotees arriving in beachwear, given that Ganpatipule is a highly popular coastal tourist destination.Vivek Bhide, a trustee of Sansthan Shreedev Ganpatipule, noted that the dress code had actually been announced nearly a year ago, with awareness boards distributed to local hotels and lodges. “However, despite repeated appeals, visitors continued to arrive at the temple in skimpy clothing, prompting the trust to strictly enforce the rules from the start of 2027,” Bhide said.Chief priest Amit Ghanvatkar emphasised that the move is intended to maintain the temple’s sanctity and uphold cultural traditions.“The decision has received widespread support from regular devotees,” he added.The strict enforcement of these guidelines is expected to pose practical challenges for tourists who often combine a temple visit with time at the adjacent beach. Visitors arriving in casual beachwear will now have to arrange for a change of clothes before seeking darshan at the temple.
Article Summary: Men and women must wear attire that extends below the knees to enter the temple. Shorts, skirts, and dresses above knee length, along with clothing featuring ‘vulgar messages’ or prints, will be strictly prohibited. Children below the age of 10 have been exempted from this rule.

Article Title: LPG leak triggers blast at Sanpada snacks shop in Navi Mumbai, 2 injured
Article Text:
A LPG cylinder leakage caused a blast at a Sanpada snacks shop on Tuesday morning.





NAVI MUMBAI: Two men sustained severe burn injuries after a LPG cylinder leakage triggered a blast at a snacks shop on the ground floor of a society in sector-1, Sanpada on Tuesday morning. The impact of the blast was so severe that the glass facade of a hospital, located about 50 feet away, was shattered. Fortunately, the patients and staff at the hospital were not hurt.Purushottam Jadhav, Divisional officer of Vashi fire station said, "At 6.13 am, the Vashi fire station received the emergency call informing about a cylinder blast at a snacks shop in Pratik CHS on sector-1, Sanpada. The fire bridge team reached the spot within 5 minutes.It was found that the blast was due to leakage in one of the three LPG cylinders kept at snacks shop. The two men working at the snacks shop sustained severe burn injuries and were rushed to NMMC hospital, Vashi. Those injured were identified as Arjun Yadav (46) who has sustained 75 precent burn injuries and Manish Yadav (26), who has sustained 90 percent burns.The blast even caused damage to two shops adjacent to the snacks shop and three other shops in the neighbouring Abhimanyu CHS. While, the glass facade of Suraj hospital located opposite to Pratik CHS was shattered due to the impact of the blast."
Article Summary: Two men sustained severe burn injuries after a LPG cylinder leakage triggered a blast at a snacks shop on the ground floor of a society in Sanpada. The impact of the blast was so severe that the glass facade of a hospital, located about 50 feet away, was shattered. Fortunately, the patients and staff at the hospital were not hurt.

Article Title: Khalapur temple theft: Video shows masked man stealing silver Padukas; 2 arrested in Pune
Article Text:
he accused stole silver Charan Paduka from Shree Swami Samarth temple on September 2





NAVI MUMBAI: The Khalapur police probing the theft case wherein a masked man had decamped with a pair of silver toe-knob sandals (Charan Paduka) representing divine footprints offered at Shree Swami Samarth temple in Khalapur city on September 2, have arrested the acccused thief and his aide by tracking them to Pune on Monday.Pradeep Rayannavar, senior inspector of Khalapur informed that, the arrested accused are Mahendrasingh Rathod, 45, who hails from Rajasthan and Ravi Soni, 32, who hails from UP and is a history-sheeter as a theft case is registered against him in Pune.Both were presently residing in Chikhali, Pune district.On September 2, the temple trustee Deepak Bodarde, 68, lodged a complaint of theft of silver Padukas from the temple.When the CCTV footage of the temple premises was checked, it was seen that a masked man wearing a hat and attired in white Kurta-Payjama entering the temple around 7.30am.He goes to the first floor of the temple where the silver Padukas were kept in front of the idol of Shree Swami Samarth.By pretending to offer prayers, he picked up the Padukas and hid them inside his Kurta and exited the temple.Inspector Rayannavar said," The theft was committed when the temple priest had gone to his room near the temple.Upon checking the CCTV footage of the roads near the temple, it was seen that two masked men on a bike were loitering near the temple and conducted a reece before committing the theft.""Considering the religious sentiments of the devotees, Raigad SP forms a special police team to detect the case at the earliest. Subsequently, the CCTV footage along the escape route of the thieves were scanned. The bike used in the crime did not have a registration number plate," Rayannavar added.He further said, "However, using technical expertise, intelligence inputs and footages of CCTV camera along the highways, the thieves on bike were tracked and apprehended from Chikhali in Pune district. We have seized from them the stolen Padukas and the bike used in the crime. On Monday, the acccused were produced before the Khalapur JMFC court that remanded them to police custody till Friday."
Article Summary: A pair of silver toe-knob sandals (Charan Paduka) representing divine footprints offered at Shree Swami Samarth temple in Khalapur city were stolen on September 2. The accused thief and his aide were arrested by tracking them to Pune on Monday.
